newsitem.title: USA: Northfield tightens blood substitute race.
newsitem.headline: Northfield tightens blood substitute race.

text.p: Northfield Laboratories Inc gained some ground Wednesday in its race to market the first human blood substitute by gaining approval for a Phase III clinical trial using its lead product, PolyHeme.

The approval granted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration will permit PolyHeme infusions in about 250 elective surgery patients and is the first granted at the Phase III level to Northfield, based in Evanston, Ill.
Northfield shares were up 1-3/8 at 12 after the announcement of the FDA action.

Rival Baxter International Inc has a similar blood substitute product, HemAssist, in Phase III trials covering trauma and surgery. The Deerfield, Ill.-based healthcare giant says it is well ahead of Northfield in the race to market.

"We're looking at a commercial launch in Europe late this year or the beginning of next year. We would expect the U.S. launch would be about a year after that. So that would be late 1998 or early 1999," said a Baxter spokeswoman.

Northfield chief executive Richard DeWoskin commented, "Baxter says they're in Phase III trials in surgery and trauma. But in neither case do they give anywhere near the dose we do. We've given more product at higher doses than anybody."
The Phase III approval for the Northfield trial is for infusions of six units, or about three liters, a dosing level with which Northfield has considerable experience.
Northfield received FDA approval in November to conduct Phase II clinical trials at a 10-unit dosing level.
DeWoskin said Northfield anticipates commercial launch of Polyheme in 1999.
To date, Northfield has received the most attention for its pursuit of the trauma market for PolyHeme, but DeWoskin said it has all along been pursuing the surgery market, too.
"We've been pursuing parallel paths for years.... This one was just the first one granted," he said.
Some other competitors in the blood substitute race have suffered setbacks.
Last month, Eli Lilly and Co said it ended its financial support for development of the Optro blood substitute product by Somatogen Inc.
Last year, Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc terminated its agreement to co-develop Hemopure, another product, with privately held Biopure Corp.
